compare.title: How big is that plane, really?
compare.lede: Pick two airliners and see them drawn at exactly the same scale. Every shape below is built from the real published length and wingspan.
compare.bothToScale: Both aircraft drawn to the same scale, seen from above.
compare.svgAlt: Top view of a {a} drawn over a {b}, both to the same scale.
compare.yardstickTitle: Things you already know the size of
compare.yardstickAlt: Bars showing everyday objects at the same scale as the aircraft above.
compare.busFact: The {plane} is about {buses} school buses long.
compare.note: Seat counts are typical two-class layouts, with the maximum all-economy figure in brackets. Wingspan varies slightly with winglet type, and range depends on how much the aircraft is carrying.

facts.AT76: Its propellers let it use short island runways where a jet simply would not fit.
facts.E190: Small enough to fill on a quiet route, big enough to feel like a proper jet.
facts.A223: Designed in Canada as the Bombardier C Series, then bought by Airbus in 2018.
facts.A20N: "neo" means new engine option — the same airframe with engines that burn about 15% less fuel.
facts.B738: Part of the best-selling airliner family ever built: over 11,000 Boeing 737s and counting.
facts.A21N: The longest single-aisle Airbus, and long-ranged enough to cross oceans.
facts.B752: Pilots love it. Big engines on a fairly small wing make it climb like nothing else.
facts.B763: The aircraft that made crossing oceans on just two engines feel normal.
facts.B789: Its carbon-fibre wings flex several metres upwards in flight. That is on purpose.
facts.A339: A rebuilt A330 with A350-style engines and new curved wingtips.
facts.A35K: Almost the whole fuselage is carbon fibre, so the cabin can be kept more humid and comfortable.
facts.B77W: One of its engines produces more thrust than both engines of a 737 combined.
facts.B748: The longest airliner ever built, at 76.3 metres nose to tail.
facts.A388: Two full-length passenger decks. No other airliner has ever managed that.

quiz.tryAgainHint: Close. Read it once more and try again — your best score is kept.

liftLab.alt: A wing seen from the side with air flowing past it and an arrow showing lift.
liftLab.notEnough: Not enough lift yet — go faster or tilt more
liftLab.stalled: Stalled. The air has stopped following the wing.
liftLab.note: Simplified on purpose. Real wings differ, but the two rules shown here are real: lift grows with the square of speed, and it collapses past about 15 degrees.

game.title: Guess the plane, guess the airport
game.lede: Five rounds. Three silhouettes to name, two airports to find on the map.
game.rule1: Aircraft are drawn to true scale — the bus underneath is 11 metres long, so size is a real clue.
game.rule2: For airports, click where you think it is. The closer you are, the more points you score.
game.rule3: 1,000 points a round, 5,000 in total. Your best score is saved.

game.scaleHint: Drawn to scale. Count the engines, and compare it with the bus.
game.clickMap: Click on the map where you think it is.
game.newBest: That is a new personal best.

guide.title: How to use this site
guide.lede: Real airliners, in the sky, right now. This takes two minutes to read, and it updates itself whenever the site gets something new.
guide.step1: You start on a world map. Press the ICN Seoul button in the row along the top.
guide.step2: Tap any aeroplane. Its flight number, aircraft type and where it is going appear on the right.
guide.step3: That tap just unlocked your first badge. You are already collecting.

section.map: Real aeroplanes flying right now. The colour tells you the height — red means it just took off or is landing, blue means it is cruising high.
section.compare: Two aircraft drawn at exactly the same scale, one on top of the other. There are {aircraft} to choose from.
section.learn: {cards} short reads. How a wing lifts 300 tonnes, why the 747 has a hump, why Seoul to New York flies over the Arctic.
section.airports: Landings filmed from real cockpits — {videos} videos across {videoAirports} airports.
section.game: {rounds} rounds, {topScore, number} points. Name aircraft from their shadow, and find airports on the map.

tip.map: Type something like KAL017 in the search box to find one plane. It is KAL017 and not KE017 for a reason — there is a card about it in Learn. There are {hubs} airport shortcuts along the top.
tip.compare: Try the A380 against the ATR 72-600 and see what happens.
tip.learn: Each one ends with three questions. Get all three and the card is marked passed. Getting it wrong costs nothing — only your best score is kept.
tip.airports: Look for Kai Tak, the Hong Kong airport that closed in 1998, where pilots turned hard at a painted checkerboard on a hillside.
tip.game: On the airport rounds you score for being close, not just for being right. A rough guess always beats no guess.

guide.logbookBody: Press Logbook at the top right. Every aeroplane you have tapped is saved there, along with how many types you have seen, how many airlines, and how many days in a row you have visited. There are {badges} badges in total.
guide.yourProgress: So far: {planes, plural, =0 {no planes yet} one {# plane} other {# planes}} spotted, {badges} of {total} badges earned.
guide.badgeTip1: The hardest one is Superjumbo — you have to find an A380 in the sky yourself and tap it.
guide.badgeTip2: Busy Day opens when you spot five different airlines in one day. Incheon in the evening is the easy way.
guide.badgeTip3: Week of Watching needs seven days in a row. You only break the run by missing a whole day, so do not panic about it.
guide.privacy: Your collection is saved only in this browser on this device. There is no account and nothing is sent anywhere. The other side of that: clearing your browsing data erases it, and it will not follow you to another device.
guide.quietSky: Late at night the sky is quiet and there is not much to see. If the map looks empty, zoom in or press one of the airport buttons along the top. Korean skies are busiest in the evening.
guide.freshness: This page counts the badges, cards, aircraft and videos straight from the site itself, so the numbers here are always the real ones.
